# Program Scope

CloudBees oversees a large scope of products. Some projects fall under the scope of the open source Jenkins project, and as such will be handled by that security team following their documented processes at https://jenkins.io/security/. Any submissions to the CloudBees HackerOne program that fall under the scope of the Jenkins project will be forwarded to that team for further analysis, and follow-up will be handled via that team. Such reported vulnerabilities MAY be subject to bounties at the discretion of the CloudBees security team.

# Within the CloudBees portfolio, the following products are in scope:

* CloudBees DevOptics (SaaS service and associated plugins)
* CloudBees Core and associated plugins
* CloudBees CodeShip (SaaS service - app.codeship.com)
* CloudBees central authentication (aka console/GrandCentral)
* CloudBees web properties (www.cloudbees.com, go.cloudbees.com)

**Please note that just because you find the same issue within multiple domains in our portfolio, it does not mean we will treat them as separate issues.  Please don't open multiple tickets for the same issue for each domain, as we will just mark them as duplicates**

# Areas of highest interest

We are most interested in, and will pay higher bounties for:
* OWASP top 10 related issues, such as demonstrated XSS
* Anything that allows bypass or gamification of the authentication system (aside from brute forcing or DoS style attacks)
* Things that would expose private user data in ways that are not intended.
* Ability to modify or inject content into any of our public web properties

# Areas of lowest interest

We are not particularly interested in:
* Blatant dumps of information from scanning tools. Do not dump your burp suite findings with links to public pages about why that finding is bad. You must demonstrate an actual exploitable issue.
* CVEs for versions of software you may identify we are running unless you can point to an actual vulnerability
* Reports of best practices you feel CloudBees should be following
* Reports involving low or medium issues surrounding our authentication/login system (including things like best practices, rate limiting, etc). We are in the process of replacing this system with a 3rd party tool, so our efforts are going towards that and not fixing anything other than high or critical vulnerabilities.  Including, but not limited to: rate limiting features, captcha bypass techniques, session/cookie management related items on things like email change, logout, password reset, etc.

* Any and all reports regarding password complexity
* DKIM/SPF/DMARC/etc settings for email of domains we own
* Clickjacking on pages with no sensitive actions.
* Unauthenticated/logout/login CSRF.
* Attacks requiring MITM or physical access to a user's device.
* Previously known vulnerable libraries without a working Proof of Concept.
* Comma Separated Values (CSV) injection without demonstrating a vulnerability.
* Missing best practices in SSL/TLS configuration.
* Any activity that could lead to the disruption of our service (DoS).
* Content spoofing and text injection issues without showing an attack vector/without being able to modify HTML/CSS

* Any type of Denial of Service
* Spamming/Messaging
* Social Engineering attempts on CloudBees employees or contractors
* Any physical attempts to access to CloudBees offices

* Follow HackerOne's [disclosure guidelines](https://www.hackerone.com/disclosure-guidelines).

From there, we triage internally with our engineering teams to take scope of severity, business impact, and how we fit any potential fixes into our work queue. attributes.title: Hardcoded Nexus Repository Credentials In Publicly Accessible Repository
attributes.vulnerability_information:
Credentials for the `cloudbees` user of the `https://nexus-internal.cloudbees.com` repository were discovered within a publicly accessible docker repository. This repository contains sensitive data, including:
* Private source code (including, for example `Cloudbees Core`, `DevOptics` and `Jenkins Enterprise`)
* Other hardcoded tokens and credentials.
* The account also seems to have permission to "promote", "release" and "drop" staging repositories.

## Impact

This issue allows an attacker to view private Cloudbees source code (including, for example `Cloudbees Core`, `DevOptics` and `Jenkins Enterprise`), and includes test releases which in some cases appear to contain hardcoded credentials and tokens.

Access to this repository could result in the theft of Intellectual Property by a competitor, as well as allowing an attacker to extract credentials/tokens for use in attacking other Cloudbees services. Access to this information also allows an attacker to view uncompiled source code including developer comments, which can aid in discovering vulnerabilities in Cloudbees software. An attacker could also attempt to promote, release or delete staging code changes to disrupt Cloudbees' software development process, potentially resulting in security issues (e.g backdoors in code) or causing downtime for Cloudbees or their customers. Information relating to other Nexus users, including usernames and IP addresses is also included within repository info, which could help an attacker target Cloudbees developers via social engineering or other attacks.

# Location
The affected docker images are `cloudbees/pse-master` and `cloudbees/pse-cjoc`, including several tags. The value is stored within the image history data, and so is accessible directly on the dockerhub site at e.g.:
https://hub.docker.com/layers/cloudbees/pse-master/latest/images/sha256-6ce17709f08d454ea6899c51ad9a66a15b31429b576dd605b6507fae988efc64 (see layer 33)

The credentials for the site https://nexus-internal.cloudbees.com are:
```
Username: FPYK5i2P
Password: 0wKG+800QLTsw30RzWUrwH3eIDIW1aHLfNVOjTvQM39l
```

Some examples of hardcoded sensitive content within this repository includes:

`https://nexus-internal.cloudbees.com/service/local/repositories/staging-4524/content/com/cloudbees/jenkins/updates/maven-slurper/3.52/maven-slurper-3.52-sources.jar`
* Contains hardcoded AWS domain, mysql db username and password 

`https://nexus-internal.cloudbees.com/service/local/repositories/staging-4602/content/org/jenkins-ci/acceptance-test-harness/1.66-cb-11/acceptance-test-harness-1.66-cb-11-sources.jar?describe=info&isLocal=true&_dc=1571832800102`
* Contains "mailtrap" credentials used for test alerts

`https://nexus-internal.cloudbees.com/service/local/repositories/staging-4331/content/com/cloudbees/jenkins/je-acceptance-test/1.17/je-acceptance-test-1.17-sources.jar`
* Contains "vcenter" credentials

# Recommendations
* Invalidate and reissue the credentials from the listed location and ensure no current job processes could result in the new credentials being exposed again
* You may wish to investigate whether an attacker could have also discovered the credentials/other tokens and used them maliciously. 
* It's not clear as to whether the `nexus-internal.cloudbees.com` domain is intended to be publicly accessible, but it may be sensible to implement IP whitelisting for this domain if possible

# Author notes:
* No files were uploaded, moved, deleted etc, and no configuration changes were made during testing, to avoid the potential for disruption of live services. As a result, the full privileges of the affected account are not known and would need to be reviewed by Cloudbees to determine any further possible impact.

attributes.title: [openid4java-shaded]
attributes.vulnerability_information:
__Hello Team__,

During my test, I found [this repository](https://github.com/cloudbees/openid4java-shaded
/) also has wiki enabled by default which allows anyone without having any administrative role can push/edit changes in the wiki section of the repository on Cloudbees's account.


__POC__: Please find the attached image. For demonstration purpose, I have created a new wiki on behalf of you. Here's the link: https://github.com/cloudbees/openid4java-shaded/wiki

{F616828}

__Solution__: You can simply fix this issue for your forked repo by going to https://github.com/cloudbees/openid4java-shaded/wiki/settings and restricting those like the image below.

{F616827}

I hope you'll take a look into this and possibly restrict this asap. Additionally, please let me know when you have a fix in place. I'll be more than happy to confirm that from my side as well.

Have a good day ahead!

__Best__,
Mohammed Israil

## Impact

.

attributes.vulnerability_information:
__Hello Team__,

During my test, I found [this repository](https://github.com/cloudbees/cjp-demo-environment/) also has wiki enabled by default which allows anyone without having any administrative role can push/edit changes in the wiki section of the repository on Cloudbees's account.


__POC__: Please find the attached image. For demonstration purpose, I have created a new wiki on behalf of you. Here's the link: https://github.com/cloudbees/cjp-demo-environment/wiki

{F616819}

__Solution__: You can simply fix this issue for your forked repo by going to https://github.com/cloudbees/cjp-demo-environment/wiki/settings and restricting those like the image below.

{F616818}

I hope you'll take a look into this and possibly restrict this asap. Additionally, please let me know when you have a fix in place. I'll be more than happy to confirm that from my side as well.

Have a good day ahead!

__Best__,
Mohammed Israil

## Impact

.

attributes.vulnerability_information:
__Hello Team__,

During my reckon process, I found your official [GitHub account](https://github.com/cloudbees/) and there, I noticed that one of your GitHub default [public wiki](https://github.com/cloudbees/JGroups/) is tuned ON which can be edit by any logged-in user without even having push privileges in the system. __POC__: Please find the attached image. For demonstration purpose, I have created a new wiki on behalf of you. Here's the link: https://github.com/cloudbees/JGroups/wiki

{F616792}

As wiki can be edited by any person on the internet, a malicious attacker can accurately craft a message or a note which would lead a user to download a malicious component in a natural way.

The user would surely trust the code (of course if he trusts the company itself), so he will extrapolate this trust to the wiki and consider it being safe enough to follow the instructions and downloading himself a malware.

__Issue__: Actually, prior to around 2015, any repositories created in GitHub, by default, had the wiki enabled, and allowed anyone to edit the wiki, even if they didn't have push/edit access to the repository. Have a good day ahead!

__Best__,
Mohammed Israil

attributes.title: Previously Created sessions continue being valid after Two-factor authentication activation
attributes.vulnerability_information:
Hi team,

I found one issue related to your 2FA system on https://app.codeship.com/user/edit

Description : 

1.access the same account on https://app.codeship.com/ -access in two devices.
2.on device 'A' go to https://app.codeship.com/user/edit > complete all steps to activate the 2FA system
Now the 2FA is activated for this account

3.back to device 'B' reload the page
The session still active

## Impact

Impact:
In this scenario when 2FA is activated the other sessions of the account are not invalidated.

2FA is required to login. I believe the expected and recommended behavior here is to terminate the other sessions> request a new login> request the 2FA code> so then give the account access again.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I tried come with the following solution :

Consider a scenario
I had shared myapp.codeship.com account with 3 persons
1-myself
2-myGF
3-mymother

I logged into app.codeship.com account with my GF's device and i forget that incident(Also that session is still alive). After some point we got broke up. Later i want to add security to my account, by enabling 2factor authentication instead of changing the passoword. Because my mother is not good at remembering password, hence i used same password for different site and i enabled 2factor authentication to protect all account from attackers. Here whenever i receive a otp message it will send to my mother's mobile also with the help of app or script or manually.

So myGF can still can access to my app.codeship.com account, also she can get password of all my personal sites by accessing the password manager.
To take revenge she might use my social media password and send some 18+ messages to my professor.

activating 2-FA only requires a second factor for new login attempts to prevent, that an attacker with only access to the password, can access this account.

I hope the logic is wrong. I tested this on multiple sites. For example: Google, 1passwordmanager, protonmail.
Since app.codeship.com is also providing password manager for the user account, it should be more secured than normal user account.
Activating 2-FA is not limited to prevent new login attempt. It also prevent existing sessions by flushing the it. So an attacker with the password can unable to access the account.

Your described finding would only mitigate the attack vector, where an attacker has already access to an account (e.g. through phishing). In these cases, your account would already be compromised and the attacker has full control over it

Consider my GF doesnt know that his device has my app.codeship.com account session. But after some time she can accidently find my account is there on her device.
OR
Eventhough attackers knows my password and monitors my device, session flushing on 2-FA would prevent the attacker from further monitoring.
Here you can see that victim doesnt aware about that his account is hacked.(Its a different scenario, dont imagine with the GF scenario which is mentioned above)

Disabling the session on 2-FA activation would not solve the issue that the attacker has access to your password (or maybe even changed it).

Yes it will not solve the issue. But prevent the attacker from further monitoring the device. It will protect the victim when he is not aware about his account is monitored by someother person also.
Hope attacker will not change the password, in the case he want to continuously monitor the activities of the victim.

Additionally, it increases the burden on the user and discourages the usage of 2-FA authentication, if after enabling of 2-FA the user has to login to all his sessions, apps and windows application again. Some user would even disable 2-FA again.

Normally users activate 2FA on considering the security in mind. Hence i hope they cant consider logging into all device as a burden. Instead they feel their accounts are placed in a secure hand.

Since app.codeship.com is an security based company, it is good to consider a fix for this logical business flaw.

attributes.name: Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Stored
attributes.description: The application stores dangerous data in a database, message forum, visitor log, or other trusted data store. At a later time, the dangerous data is subsequently read back into the application and included in dynamic content. From an attacker's perspective, the optimal place to inject malicious content is in an area that is displayed to either many users or particularly interesting users. Interesting users typically have elevated privileges in the application or interact with sensitive data that is valuable to the attacker. If one of these users executes malicious content, the attacker may be able to perform privileged operations on behalf of the user or gain access to sensitive data belonging to the user. For example, the attacker might inject XSS into a log message, which might not be handled properly when an administrator views the logs.

attributes.policy:
CloudBees takes security very seriously and investigates all reported vulnerabilities. We want to keep our software and services safe for everybody. We welcome working with the security community to resolve valid issues promptly.

# Bounty Program
CloudBees offers monetary bounties for reports of qualifying security vulnerabilities. Reward amounts will vary based on the severity of the report, and eligibility is at our sole discretion. Not all submitted items will be in scope for a reward. Duplicate issues will be merged.

Our determination of what is in scope or not is final. Awarded bounties are not negotiable, including the decision to not pay out a bounty.

# Program Scope

CloudBees oversees a large scope of products. Some projects fall under the scope of the open source Jenkins project, and as such will be handled by that security team following their documented processes at https://jenkins.io/security/. Any submissions to the CloudBees HackerOne program that fall under the scope of the Jenkins project will be forwarded to that team for further analysis, and follow-up will be handled via that team. Such reported vulnerabilities MAY be subject to bounties at the discretion of the CloudBees security team.

# Within the CloudBees portfolio, the following products are in scope:

* CloudBees DevOptics (SaaS service and associated plugins)
* CloudBees Core and associated plugins
* CloudBees CodeShip (SaaS service - app.codeship.com)
* CloudBees central authentication (aka console/GrandCentral)
* CloudBees web properties (www.cloudbees.com, go.cloudbees.com)

**Please note that just because you find the same issue within multiple domains in our portfolio, it does not mean we will treat them as separate issues.  Please don't open multiple tickets for the same issue for each domain, as we will just mark them as duplicates**

# Areas of highest interest

We are most interested in, and will pay higher bounties for:
* OWASP top 10 related issues, such as demonstrated XSS
* Anything that allows bypass or gamification of the authentication system (aside from brute forcing or DoS style attacks)
* Things that would expose private user data in ways that are not intended.
* Ability to modify or inject content into any of our public web properties

# Areas of lowest interest

We are not particularly interested in:
* Blatant dumps of information from scanning tools. Do not dump your burp suite findings with links to public pages about why that finding is bad. You must demonstrate an actual exploitable issue.
* CVEs for versions of software you may identify we are running unless you can point to an actual vulnerability
* Reports of best practices you feel CloudBees should be following
* Reports involving low or medium issues surrounding our authentication/login system (including things like best practices, rate limiting, etc). We are in the process of replacing this system with a 3rd party tool, so our efforts are going towards that and not fixing anything other than high or critical vulnerabilities.  Including, but not limited to: rate limiting features, captcha bypass techniques, session/cookie management related items on things like email change, logout, password reset, etc.

# Common Reports we get that are out of scope
* Any and all reports regarding password complexity
* DKIM/SPF/DMARC/etc settings for email of domains we own
* Clickjacking on pages with no sensitive actions.
* Unauthenticated/logout/login CSRF.
* Attacks requiring MITM or physical access to a user's device.
* Previously known vulnerable libraries without a working Proof of Concept.
* Comma Separated Values (CSV) injection without demonstrating a vulnerability.
* Missing best practices in SSL/TLS configuration.
* Any activity that could lead to the disruption of our service (DoS).
* Content spoofing and text injection issues without showing an attack vector/without being able to modify HTML/CSS
* Open redirects unless there's an actual security issue associated with it. Manually changing the URL in a redirect is not sufficient cause for a security issue. Tampering with an existing redirect that legitimately tricks an actual user to a different site IS valid.

# While researching we ask that you do not perform the following:
* Any type of Denial of Service
* Spamming/Messaging
* Social Engineering attempts on CloudBees employees or contractors
* Any physical attempts to access to CloudBees offices

# Disclosure Policy
* As this is a private program, please do not discuss this program or any vulnerabilities (even resolved ones) outside of the program without express consent from the organization.
* Follow HackerOne's [disclosure guidelines](https://www.hackerone.com/disclosure-guidelines).

# What to expect from us
* Our goal is to triage and accept your deny your report within two US business days.  From there, we triage internally with our engineering teams to take scope of severity, business impact, and how we fit any potential fixes into our work queue. Please note that most reported items are not business critical, and as such it takes some time for our teams to determine exactly the scope of the issue, and how it will be addressed.  Once we have a good idea of how it will be fixed and the overall severity, we will pay a bounty. Our preference is to pay a bounty at the same time we validate resolution of the issue as it allows us to make sure the amount of the bounty is appropriately tied to the actual problem.
* In some cases the item filed may be (by our team) considered more of a bug than a security issue. We may still elect to fix and pay out bounties for such items, but there is no particular timeline for addressing them as our product management teams will be scoping them into the product plan details.
* While we appreciate your reports, asking the status of when we will respond, fix the item, or post a bounty will not receive a response. Repeated attempts at asking for status of such reports may result in banning from continued participation in our program.

This program page may be updated at any time.
